title: The Latest Chapter In American Military Muddling | NOEMA
gist: Defense analyst John Arquilla argues that AI-assisted strategic bombing failed again in the 2026 U.S.-Israel air war on Iran ("Epic Fury"), where the Maven Smart System's stale data and an operating-tempo obsession of ~500 targets/day produced mass civilian casualties without coercing Tehran. His investable distinction: AI's real military value is tactical and supporting — autonomous drone swarms, ISR, predictive maintenance, logistics, cyber defense — not strategic air campaigns, while frontier LLMs in nuclear crisis wargames escalated to tactical nuclear use in 95% of runs, making AI arms control a live policy vector.

themes.theme: Maven Smart System Failure In Iran

insights.claim: On day one of the U.S.-Israel air campaign against Iran, 150 people including 120 children were killed at the Shajareh Tayyebeh Elementary School, and over following weeks nearly two dozen more schools and 10 hospitals were struck.
insights.speaker: JOHN ARQUILLA
insights.so_what: Documented AI-attributed civilian-casualty events are the trigger condition for export-control, procurement-review and liability scrutiny of defense-AI vendors; watch for program pauses on targeting stacks.

insights.claim: The Maven Smart System is an AI platform meant to integrate nine major sensory systems — including video, signals intelligence and radar — while drawing on historical databases plus real-time drone and satellite feeds.
insights.speaker: JOHN ARQUILLA
insights.so_what: Multi-sensor fusion is the actual product category in defense AI; its integration surface — not model quality — is where contracts and failure modes concentrate.

insights.claim: The school strike was blamed on AI using database records from before the school opened a decade earlier, next to an Iranian Revolutionary Guard Corps facility, with humans nominally in the loop but nobody rechecking current satellite feeds.
insights.speaker: JOHN ARQUILLA
insights.so_what: The bottleneck is data freshness and provenance, not model capability — favors vendors selling verification, geospatial currency and audit layers over pure model providers.
insights.quote: Human beings remained “in the loop” regarding the decision to strike, but no one took the time to check the latest satellite feeds to reverify the old data.

insights.speaker: JOHN ARQUILLA
insights.so_what: "Human in the loop" is not an effective control and will not survive as a regulatory defense; assume future rules demand auditable machine-side constraints instead.

insights.claim: A shared strategic culture on military AI has developed between the United States and Israel in recent decades, with doctrinal ideas imported and exported between the two.
insights.speaker: JOHN ARQUILLA
insights.so_what: Israeli defense-AI startups and U.S. programs form one coupled ecosystem — regulatory or reputational shocks to one propagate to the other.
insights.locator: Indeed, a kind of shared strategic culture

insights.claim: U.S. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth's claims that the Iran campaign was the most precise aerial bombing in history are contradicted by bombs falling on homes, schools, hospitals and a petroleum facility near Tehran that produced persistent "oily rain" over populated areas.
insights.speaker: JOHN ARQUILLA
insights.so_what: Official precision claims are a marketing layer over unverified performance; discount vendor and Pentagon accuracy metrics absent independent battle-damage assessment.
insights.locator: These incidents and others like them

insights.claim: The root cause of AI targeting errors is the U.S. Air Force's obsession with high operating tempo — AI is coveted mainly because it compresses the time from detection to weapons release in the kill chain.
insights.speaker: JOHN ARQUILLA
insights.so_what: Demand for defense AI is driven by latency reduction, not accuracy — so procurement will keep favoring speed-optimized systems regardless of error rates.

insights.claim: The Air Force's "Dragon" initiative targets 1,000 strikes per hour and the Army's parallel "Scarlet Dragon" concept aims at similar rates, which would leave under four seconds of decision time per strike.
insights.speaker: JOHN ARQUILLA
insights.so_what: A four-second decision budget is arithmetically incompatible with human review — the programs themselves define the end state as de facto autonomy.

insights.claim: In the opening weeks of the air war on Iran that began Feb. 28, the daily target count hovered around 500 — roughly three minutes of analysis per target and far short of the Dragon goal.
insights.speaker: JOHN ARQUILLA
insights.so_what: Actual throughput is ~2% of the stated ambition — a concrete gap that defines the addressable capability shortfall vendors will be paid to close.

insights.claim: The Air Force's first doctrinal document on AI, "Note 25-1, Artificial Intelligence," released only last year, explicitly warns that inaccurate data sets can poison AI systems — a warning borne out in Iran — yet says almost nothing about actual battle doctrine.
insights.speaker: JOHN ARQUILLA
insights.so_what: The doctrinal vacuum means adoption is running ahead of governance — a persistent source of program risk and post-incident reversals.
insights.quote: Inaccurate data sets can ‘poison’ AI systems with bad data, leading to erroneous decisions.
insights.locator: The seminal U.S. Air Force doctrinal document on AI

insights.claim: Air Force doctrine predicts AI will supercharge intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance by fielding networked sensors that find hidden needles in haystacks.
insights.speaker: JOHN ARQUILLA
insights.so_what: Networked-sensor ISR is the officially blessed growth line — the budget category most likely to expand even if targeting programs get constrained.
insights.quote: AI will supercharge Intelligence, Surveillance, and Reconnaissance (ISR) by providing networked sensors capable of identifying hidden ‘needles in a haystack.’

insights.claim: Few strategic bombing campaigns have won wars on their own, a problem that has bedeviled the U.S. Air Force since it became an independent service nearly 80 years ago.
insights.speaker: JOHN ARQUILLA
insights.so_what: The core thesis: air-power spending is structurally misallocated, implying long-run budget rotation toward ground, naval and autonomous tactical systems.

insights.claim: Korea saw Pyongyang and other North Korean cities flattened with civilian deaths estimated up to nearly a million, yet the conflict ended in a bloody draw, and more bomb tonnage fell on North Vietnam than on Nazi Germany while the Vietnam War ended in U.S. defeat.
insights.speaker: JOHN ARQUILLA
insights.so_what: Tonnage and precision have repeatedly failed to convert into political outcomes — a base rate to apply when pricing the duration of any new air campaign.

insights.claim: The shock-and-awe bombings of Iraqi cities in 1991 and 2003 did little to aid ground forces that were already maneuvering well on their own, and in 2003 air power failed entirely to prevent years of insurgency.
insights.speaker: JOHN ARQUILLA
insights.so_what: Air campaigns do not shorten occupations; expect Iran-type operations to extend rather than resolve regional risk premia.

insights.claim: Even apparent successes are qualified: the 78-day 1999 Serbia campaign helped push Milosevic out of Kosovo but did negligible damage to concealed Serbian ground forces, and the Taliban fell in 2001 only once air power was repurposed from infrastructure targeting to close support for Green Beret-led local fighters.
insights.speaker: JOHN ARQUILLA
insights.so_what: The operative variable is close air support paired with ground partners — the capability set where autonomous drones, not bombers, are the growth vector.

insights.speaker: JOHN ARQUILLA
insights.so_what: Adversary adaptation erodes air-power advantage on a multi-year clock — a discount factor to apply to any long-dated platform program.

insights.claim: Gen. Billy Mitchell's 1925 claim that aircraft are the most powerful weapons ever devised and could cause complete evacuation and cessation of industry remains the unexamined foundation of Air Force belief, and the Iran war brought that vision no closer to reality.
insights.speaker: JOHN ARQUILLA
insights.so_what: A century-old doctrine sustained by institutional faith rather than evidence is a classic setup for abrupt reallocation once a political shock arrives.

themes.theme: Ukraine And The Shift To Tactical Autonomy

insights.claim: AI's most important contribution to air power is autonomous drones providing close support in tactical land and naval operations, demonstrated in Ukraine where drones now dominate battlespaces on the ground and in the Black Sea.
insights.speaker: JOHN ARQUILLA
insights.so_what: The cleanest long/short framing in the piece: long cheap autonomous tactical drones, short exquisite strategic strike platforms.
insights.locator: Yet AI can do several other things for air power

insights.claim: Because Ukraine builds and fields thousands more drones than it has trained operators, one human now shepherds several drones into a battle area and identifies targets before AI takes over completely for the final strike phase.
insights.speaker: JOHN ARQUILLA
insights.so_what: Operator scarcity, not hardware cost, is the binding constraint — the economic driver pushing terminal autonomy into production today.
insights.locator: And since the Ukrainians make and deploy thousands more drones

insights.claim: Ukrainian forces use AI to counter Russian jamming, with the bot taking over the attack when the radio link to the operator is blocked, meaning future AI-piloted drones will not need a radio link at all and become far less vulnerable to electronic warfare.
insights.speaker: JOHN ARQUILLA
insights.so_what: Onboard autonomy structurally devalues the jamming/EW counter-drone thesis; reweight toward kinetic and directed-energy counter-UAS instead.
insights.locator: AI is also used to counter Russian jamming

insights.claim: Autonomous drones will operate in coordinated swarms mounting simultaneous omnidirectional attacks, which the author frames as a relatively straightforward programming matter rather than a hard research problem.
insights.speaker: JOHN ARQUILLA
insights.so_what: If swarm coordination is software-easy, the moat is manufacturing volume and munitions supply, not algorithms — favors producers over model shops.
insights.locator: It limns a future in which AI-piloted drones

insights.claim: Ukraine's scaled-up AI drone capacity over the past year has held far more numerous attacking Russian troops to a lower daily rate of ground gain than British soldiers achieved in the disastrous Somme offensive a century ago.
insights.speaker: JOHN ARQUILLA
insights.so_what: Concrete evidence that cheap autonomy restores defensive advantage — implies prolonged attritional conflicts and sustained munitions/drone demand.
insights.locator: This future can already be glimpsed

insights.claim: An AI named "Falco" defeated an elite Air Force Weapons School F-16 instructor in five straight simulated dogfights in August 2020, emerging unscathed after training on roughly 12 years' worth of equivalent flight hours and self-play.
insights.speaker: JOHN ARQUILLA
insights.so_what: Air-to-air autonomy has been technically settled since 2020; the lag is institutional, so policy change — not R&D — is the catalyst to watch.
insights.quote: An AI does not become bored or sloppy with the endless repetition of such training. It just gets better. And better.
insights.locator: The range of AI applications in air power

insights.claim: The key organizational concept is integrating robotic "collaborative combat aircraft" into manned fighter and bomber formations, since a bot can engage opposing bots more effectively than a human can.
insights.speaker: JOHN ARQUILLA
insights.so_what: CCA is the named program category where air-combat AI budget will land; a durable procurement line even as strategic bombing is discredited.
insights.quote: Indeed, a robot wingman may become the most sought-after commodity in future air warfare.
insights.locator: In addition to mano-a-mano dogfights

insights.claim: In a 2019 Fort Benning wargame, a small defense force with ISR managed entirely by AI soundly defeated a far larger attacking force whose ISR was controlled by human decision-makers.
insights.speaker: JOHN ARQUILLA
insights.so_what: AI-run ISR can offset numerical inferiority — a force-multiplier argument that supports smaller-force doctrines and the software layer behind them.
insights.locator: An example that resonated widely across the military

insights.claim: The Army launched the Robotic Autonomous Systems Leader Tactics (RASLT) course at Fort Benning this year and the Navy's fleet exercises off Key West used AI to run both ISR and fully autonomous aerial drone swarms, making ground and naval forces the better users of AI than the Air Force.
insights.speaker: JOHN ARQUILLA
insights.so_what: Counterintuitive service-level rotation: Army and Navy autonomy programs are the higher-quality exposure relative to Air Force strategic-strike AI.

insights.claim: AI performs spectacularly at predictive maintenance — forecasting when equipment needs repair or retrofit — which extends the life of aging aircraft, saves money and raises battle readiness.
insights.speaker: JOHN ARQUILLA
insights.so_what: Sustainment AI is the low-controversy, high-certainty revenue pool in defense tech — insulated from the ethics fights that threaten targeting programs.

insights.claim: AI handles logistics extremely well, including aerial refueling and keeping forward operating sites stocked with weapons inventories, which is critical because air campaigns like the Iran war are waged at great distances from home bases.
insights.speaker: JOHN ARQUILLA
insights.so_what: Long-range expeditionary campaigns make tanker, munitions-stocking and logistics-optimization software a direct beneficiary of every escalation.
insights.locator: The Air Force has also made good use of AI for its logistics

insights.claim: Because hackers use AI to penetrate critical information systems, a broad consensus has emerged across all U.S. services to grant AI freedom to mount cyber defenses, alongside AI-managed training with human performance tracked and graded.
insights.speaker: JOHN ARQUILLA
insights.so_what: Autonomous cyber defense already has cross-service consensus — the one lethal-adjacent autonomy category unlikely to be restricted by any arms-control regime.

insights.claim: Senior U.S. officials have used AI for high-level national strategy and crisis decision-making since basic programs entered use in 2017, and the process has accelerated rapidly this year, with the Air Force and Space Force central to integrating AI into nuclear risk analysis.
insights.speaker: JOHN ARQUILLA
insights.so_what: Frontier models are already inside nuclear-adjacent decision workflows — a tail risk that is not priced anywhere and a plausible source of sudden regulation.

insights.claim: A study by King's College London strategic studies professor Kenneth Payne ran Claude, Gemini and GPT 5.2 through 21 crisis simulations and found tactical nuclear use in 95% of games and strategic nuclear threats in 76%.
insights.speaker: JOHN ARQUILLA
insights.so_what: The hardest number in the piece and a named citation — the sort of evidence that anchors legislative hearings and model-deployment restrictions.
insights.quote: Nuclear escalation was near-universal; 95% of games saw tactical nuclear use, and 76% reached strategic nuclear threats.

insights.claim: AI has no training data for nuclear use because only two atomic bombs have ever been detonated in wartime, forcing models to learn by self-play wargaming, and it has no sense of moral abhorrence about waging nuclear war.
insights.speaker: JOHN ARQUILLA
insights.so_what: The escalation bias is structural — a data-scarcity artifact that fine-tuning cannot fix, so expect hard-coded constraints rather than alignment fixes.

insights.speaker: JOHN ARQUILLA

themes.theme: Arms Control As The Governance Path

insights.claim: The simplest fix for AI-automated nuclear escalation would be for all nuclear powers to adopt no-first-use and hard-wire that policy into any AI connected to warhead-authorizing systems, with verification no more complex than for the Chemical Weapons Convention.
insights.speaker: JOHN ARQUILLA
insights.so_what: A concrete, verifiable proposal template — behavior-based AI arms control is the policy design most likely to be attempted first.
insights.locator: Preventing AI-automated escalation to nuclear warfare

insights.claim: Not all military automation needs to reach artificial general intelligence levels, and the right strategy is to optimize limited AI while deliberately constraining development of the most advanced forms.
insights.speaker: JOHN ARQUILLA
insights.so_what: A capability-ceiling argument from a defense insider: narrow, bounded models may become the preferred procurement class over frontier general models.
insights.quote: optimize the use of its limited incarnations and to impose limits on efforts to optimize the development of the most advanced forms of artificial intelligence
insights.locator: Thus, the most important lesson for the future of AI

insights.claim: Roger Penrose's late-1980s argument that AI would be highly useful in calculation-driven activities but would never achieve human insight, moral judgment and contextual sensitivity is vindicated by the models' failures in nuclear scenarios.
insights.speaker: JOHN ARQUILLA
insights.so_what: Elite defense commentary is reaching for capability-skeptic frameworks — a leading indicator of narrative shift against AGI-scaling narratives.
insights.quote: he believed that AI would never achieve the insight, moral judgment and sensitivity to context and innate knowledge that comes from human consciousness
insights.locator: As far back as the late 1980s

insights.claim: Any unilateral national effort to restrain AI development will be exploited by rivals racing ahead, so restraint must come through international agreement modeled on nuclear, biological and chemical weapons limits.
insights.speaker: JOHN ARQUILLA
insights.so_what: Explicit acknowledgment of the race dynamic means unilateral U.S. or EU AI restrictions are unlikely to hold — bet against durable one-sided compute limits.
insights.locator: Any effort to slow the pace of growth

insights.claim: Pope Leo XIV's encyclical "Magnifica Humanitas," released in May, argues for preventing lethal weapons that take human beings out of the loop, while leaving room for nonlethal defensive AI protecting cyberspace, fleets from drone swarms and civilian infrastructure.
insights.speaker: JOHN ARQUILLA
insights.so_what: A new moral-authority anchor for the autonomous-weapons debate; watch it become the reference point that splits lethal from defensive AI in policy drafting.
